# The exact Bernoulli transform and a false larger Laplace class

The first reformulation below is exact for actual two-positive simplex
sections. The last section rigorously falsifies a tempting enlargement;
it does not falsify the original geometric inequality.

## 1. A single Poisson-binomial law

Use the parameters p>q, h=1-q/p, a_j=r_j/(q+r_j), rho, and L from
`candidate f942bc6e02fdf1dd`.
Let N be a sum of independent Bernoulli variables of success probabilities
a_j. Put

    M(z)=E z^N=product_j(1-a_j+a_j z),
    mu=EN=sum a_j, p0=Pr(N=0)=product_j(1-a_j),
    t=q/p=1-h.

Then rho=M(t), L=h rho/(1-rho), X=p0/rho, and the exact omitted-p
variance inequality is

    (1-L mu) M(1+L)
      >=(1-t rho)[1-p0(1-t rho)/(h rho)].             (1)

This is just the formulas for the actual cap and section means, with no
independence assumption on those means. In particular the generating
function M retains the same a_j in every term.

## 2. A sum of scaled exponentials

Let E_j be independent unit-rate exponential variables and put
T=sum_j a_j E_j. Direct Laplace transformation gives

    1/M(z)=E exp(-(z-1)T)

whenever the expectation is finite. In particular

    rho=1/E exp(hT), p0=1/E exp(T), mu=ET,
    L=h/[E exp(hT)-1], M(1+L)=1/E exp(-LT).          (2)

All these expectations are finite for the actual class because 0<a_j<1
and 0<h<1. Thus (1) is an exact four-moment formulation for sums of
independent scaled exponentials. No assertion for arbitrary nonnegative
T follows from (2).

## 3. An exact obstruction to dropping the sum-of-exponentials hypothesis

Set h=1/2, epsilon=2^(-30), and take the two-point law

    T=log 2 with probability 1-epsilon,
    T=40 log 2 with probability epsilon.

Define u=2[E exp(T/2)-1]=1/L, b=E exp(T). Under the formal substitutions
(2), the two sides of (1) become respectively

    A=(1-ET/u)/E exp(-T/u),
    B=(1+u)/(2+u) [1-(1+u)/b].                      (3)

They satisfy A<1/2 and B>3/5, so (1) fails strictly for this law.

Here are rational certificates for every estimate. Since
141/100<sqrt(2)<71/50, epsilon<1/1000, and
epsilon*2^20=1/1024<1/1000, direct evaluation gives

    41/50<u<421/500, b>1024.

The lower u bound remains valid after subtracting epsilon sqrt(2):
sqrt(2)>707/500 and epsilon sqrt(2)<1/1000 give
E exp(T/2)>1413/1000>141/100. Also log2>69/100;
for example the positive expansion
log2=2 sum_(k>=0) [1/(2k+1)](1/3)^(2k+1)
already proves this from its first three terms. Therefore ET>69/100.

Since 1/u<50/41<5/4,

    E exp(-T/u)>(1-epsilon) 2^(-5/4)>399/1000.

For the last estimate, 2^(-5/4)>2/5 follows by taking fourth powers,
and (1-1/1000)(2/5)=999/2500>399/1000. Hence

    A < (76/421)/(399/1000)<1/2,

where the last inequality is 152000<167979. On the other hand

    B > (91/141)(511/512)>3/5,

using u>41/50, 1+u<2, and b>1024. The last inequality is the integer
comparison 232505>216576.

This two-point law is not asserted to have the representation in
Section 2. It rules out a proof that uses only nonnegativity of T and
the four displayed exponential moments while forgetting that actual
T is a sum of independent scaled exponentials.
